The [third season](Stranger_Things_(season_3) "Stranger Things (season 3)") is set several months later, in the days leading up to the [Fourth of July celebration](Independence_Day_(United_States) "Independence Day (United States)") in 1985. Hopper becomes increasingly concerned about Eleven and Mike's relationship and becomes very protective of his daughter. Unbeknownst to the town, a secret <Soviet> laboratory underneath Starcourt seeks to open the gateway to the Upside Down. Meanwhile, the Mind Flayer uses mind control to make Billy do his bidding.[[9]](Stranger_Things#cite_note-9)[[10]](Stranger_Things#cite_note-10)

The [fourth season](Stranger_Things_(season_4) "Stranger Things (season 4)") is set several months later, in March 1986. Joyce, Will, Eleven, and Jonathan have moved to Lenora, California for a fresh start. In California, Eleven struggles with the loss of her powers and being bullied in school. Meanwhile, in Hawkins, a being from the Upside Down—an entity later dubbed Vecna—begins killing the residents of Hawkins, opening new gates between the two worlds in the process. Planning to stop Vecna, Dr. Sam Owens takes Eleven to a facility to help her regain her powers. Simultaneously, Joyce and Murray fly to Russia to rescue Hopper from the <Gulag> in [Kamchatka](Kamchatka_Peninsula "Kamchatka Peninsula").

The Korean and English language title logos incorporated the circle, triangle and square shapes into their design.

Throughout the series, the trio of circle, triangle, and square shapes appear frequently on the cards given to recruit players, on the guards' masks, and inside the show's title. These are shapes associated with the playing field for the children's game of [Squid](Squid_(game) "Squid (game)") (*Ojing-eo*). They are also used to represent the hierarchy of the guards within the complex. Following from the comparison with an [ant colony](Ant_colony "Ant colony"), the guards with circles are considered the workers, triangles as the soldiers, and squares as the managers (see also: [Korean honorifics](Korean_honorifics "Korean honorifics")). Further, in the Korean alphabet, <Hangul>, the circle represents the romanized letter "O", the triangle represents part of the letter "J", and the square represents the letter "M"; together, "OJM" are the romanized initials of *Ojing-eo Geim*, the Korean translation of *Squid Game*.[[84]](Squid_Game#cite_note-91)

Two classical music pieces are also used throughout the show as part of the players' routine: the third movement of [Joseph Haydn](Joseph_Haydn "Joseph Haydn")'s "[Trumpet Concerto](Trumpet_Concerto_(Haydn) "Trumpet Concerto (Haydn)")" is used to wake the players, and [Johann Strauss II](Johann_Strauss_II "Johann Strauss II")'s "[The Blue Danube](The_Blue_Danube "The Blue Danube")" is used to indicate the start of a new game.[[88]](Squid_Game#cite_note-bbc_musicmag-95) [Ludwig van Beethoven](Ludwig_van_Beethoven "Ludwig van Beethoven")'s "[Fifth Symphony](Symphony_No._5_(Beethoven) "Symphony No. 5 (Beethoven)")" is also heard in the VIP lounge.[[88]](Squid_Game#cite_note-bbc_musicmag-95) A cover of "[Fly Me to the Moon](Fly_Me_to_the_Moon "Fly Me to the Moon")",[[lower-alpha 8]](Squid_Game#cite_note-97) arranged by Jung and sung by Korean artist Joo Won Shin, was used over the "Red Light, Green Light" game of the first episode; according to Joo, Hwang wanted a contrast between the brutal killing of the players and the "romantic and beautiful lyrics and melody" of the song, such that the scene "embodies the increasingly polarized capitalist society that we live in today in a very compressed and cynical way".[[90]](Squid_Game#cite_note-98)

## Release

A first teaser trailer for *Wednesday* was released on August 17, 2022,[[61]](Wednesday_(TV_series)#cite_note-61) followed by a full trailer on October 9[[62]](Wednesday_(TV_series)#cite_note-62) and the unveiling of the series' opening sequence on November 8.[[63]](Wednesday_(TV_series)#cite_note-63) *Wednesday* premiered on November 16, 2022, at Hollywood Legion Theater in [Los Angeles](Los_Angeles "Los Angeles").[[64]](Wednesday_(TV_series)#cite_note-64)[[65]](Wednesday_(TV_series)#cite_note-65) Its eight episodes were released on <Netflix> on November 23, 2022.[[66]](Wednesday_(TV_series)#cite_note-Nov2023-66) In December 2022, Netflix released a promotional video to its <Twitter> account depicting [Thing](Thing_(The_Addams_Family) "Thing (The Addams Family)"), a sentient disembodied hand appearing in the series, roaming the streets of [New York City](New_York_City "New York City") and capturing passersby's reactions.[[67]](Wednesday_(TV_series)#cite_note-67)

## Reception

### Audience viewership

According to data from users of [TV Time](TV_Time "TV Time") collected by [Whip Media](Whip_Media "Whip Media"), *Wednesday* had the second-most pre-release followers of any Netflix original series on the platform, behind only *[The Witcher](The_Witcher_(TV_series) "The Witcher (TV series)")*;[[68]](Wednesday_(TV_series)#cite_note-68) it ultimately debuted at number one on Netflix in 83 countries.[[69]](Wednesday_(TV_series)#cite_note-69) The series holds the record of most hours viewed in a week for an English-language Netflix series with a total 341 million hours watched in its first week of release, amounting to more than 50 million households, and passing prior record holder *[Stranger Things 4](Stranger_Things_(season_4) "Stranger Things (season 4)")*'s 335 million hours.[[70]](Wednesday_(TV_series)#cite_note-70) [Nielsen Media Research](Nielsen_Media_Research "Nielsen Media Research") reported a combined watch time of 6 billion minutes within its first week of release, making it the second-biggest streaming week ever recorded by the firm.[[71]](Wednesday_(TV_series)#cite_note-71) Three weeks after its release, it became the second-most watched English-language Netflix series in the history of the platform, reaching an estimated 150 million households and totaling 1 billion viewing hours.[[72]](Wednesday_(TV_series)#cite_note-72) Jacob Stolworthy of *[The Independent](The_Independent "The Independent")* called the series's popularity "unprecedented" and suggested that it could jumpstart development of several other spin-off television series.[[73]](Wednesday_(TV_series)#cite_note-73)

### Controversies

On September 23, 2022, Netflix removed the series' "<LGBTQ>" tag after backlash on social media.[[45]](Dahmer_%E2%80%93_Monster%3A_The_Jeffrey_Dahmer_Story#cite_note-47)[[46]](Dahmer_%E2%80%93_Monster%3A_The_Jeffrey_Dahmer_Story#cite_note-48)

The series also received backlash from the families of Dahmer's victims, accusing Netflix of profiting off their traumatic experiences and "retraumatizing [the families] all over again". Eric Perry, a relative of victim Errol Lindsey, stated that "I want people to understand this is not just a story or historical fact, these are real people’s lives. [Lindsey] was someone’s son, someone’s brother, someone’s father, someone’s friend that was ripped from [our] lives".[[26]](Dahmer_%E2%80%93_Monster%3A_The_Jeffrey_Dahmer_Story#cite_note-LA1-28)

Production assistant Kim Alsup alleged mistreatment while on set. She stated she was one of two Black crew members [below the line](Below_the_line_(filmmaking) "Below the line (filmmaking)") on *Dahmer*, adding that "I was always being called someone else’s name, the only other Black girl who looked nothing like me, and I learned the names for 300 background extras". Alsup also alleged an "exhausting" and "unsupportive environment," stating there were no [therapists](Therapists "Therapists") on set. A spokesperson for Netflix countered this allegation, stating that everyone on set had access to free health and wellness sources, including access to a therapist.[[26]](Dahmer_%E2%80%93_Monster%3A_The_Jeffrey_Dahmer_Story#cite_note-LA1-28)

Shirley Hughes, the mother of Tony Hughes, whose story is told in the sixth episode, spoke out against the series' depiction of events. "It didn't happen like that," Hughes told *[The Guardian](The_Guardian "The Guardian")*.[[47]](Dahmer_%E2%80%93_Monster%3A_The_Jeffrey_Dahmer_Story#cite_note-49)

## Future

Having initially ordered the program in 2020 as a [limited series](Limited-run_series "Limited-run series"),[[1]](Dahmer_%E2%80%93_Monster%3A_The_Jeffrey_Dahmer_Story#cite_note-deadline-dahmer-order-2) Netflix announced on November 7, 2022, that it had renewed *Monster* as an anthology series, with two further editions based on the lives of "other monstrous figures" to be announced.[[48]](Dahmer_%E2%80%93_Monster%3A_The_Jeffrey_Dahmer_Story#cite_note-50)

On May 1, 2023, Netflix announced the second season of the series titled *Monsters: The Lyle and Erik Menéndez Story* (2024), which is based on the murder case of the [Menéndez brothers](Lyle_and_Erik_Men%C3%A9ndez "Lyle and Erik Menéndez").[[49]](Dahmer_%E2%80%93_Monster%3A_The_Jeffrey_Dahmer_Story#cite_note-51) On June 29, 2023, *[Deadline Hollywood](Deadline_Hollywood "Deadline Hollywood")* reported that Cooper Koch and [Nicholas Chavez](Nicholas_Chavez "Nicholas Chavez") were cast as Lyle and Erik Menéndez respectively.[[3]](Dahmer_%E2%80%93_Monster%3A_The_Jeffrey_Dahmer_Story#cite_note-Deadline-S2-4)

### Critical response

The [review aggregator](Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes") reported a 55% approval rating with an average rating of 6.3/10, based on 29 critic reviews. The website's critics consensus reads, "While *Monster* is seemingly self-aware of the peril in glorifying Jeffrey Dahmer, creator Ryan Murphy's salacious style nevertheless tilts this horror story into the realm of queasy exploitation."[[22]](Dahmer_%E2%80%93_Monster%3A_The_Jeffrey_Dahmer_Story#cite_note-24) <Metacritic>, which uses a weighted average, assigned a score of 46 out of 100 based on 9 critics, indicating "mixed or average reviews".[[23]](Dahmer_%E2%80%93_Monster%3A_The_Jeffrey_Dahmer_Story#cite_note-25)

Kayla Cobb at *[Decider](Decider_(website) "Decider (website)")* said the show "isn't just well directed, written, and acted. The series was initially intended as a limited series to be told in two parts. It had its original run of 15 episodes on Spanish network [Antena 3](Antena_3_(Spain) "Antena 3 (Spain)") from 2 May 2017 through 23 November 2017. acquired global streaming rights in late 2017. ## Production

### Conception and writing

Further information: [§ Themes and analysis](Money_Heist#Themes_and_analysis)
> We wanted to make a very small project in a simple way; we wanted to cross lines we couldn't cross in previous projects, in terms of narrative and structure without any intermediaries.

—Writer Esther Martinez Lobato, October 2018[[10]](Money_Heist#cite_note-dramaquarterly_181015-13)

The series was conceived by screenwriter [Álex Pina](%C3%81lex_Pina "Álex Pina") and director Jesús Colmenar during their years of collaboration since 2008.[[11]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elperiodico_190718-14) After finishing their work on the Spanish prison drama *[Locked Up](Locked_Up_(TV_series) "Locked Up (TV series)")* (*Vis a vis*), they left Globomedia to set up their own production company, named Vancouver Media, in 2016.[[11]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elperiodico_190718-14)[[12]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elespanol_170522-15) For their first project, they considered either filming a comedy or developing a heist story for television,[[11]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elperiodico_190718-14) with the latter having never been attempted before on Spanish television.[[13]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elconfidencial_170103-16) Along with former *Locked Up* colleagues,[[lower-alpha 4]](Money_Heist#cite_note-17) they developed *Money Heist* as a passion project to try new things without outside interference.[[10]](Money_Heist#cite_note-dramaquarterly_181015-13) Pina was firm about making it a limited series, feeling that dilution had become a problem for his previous productions.[[14]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_171016-18)

Initially entitled *Los Desahuciados* (*The Evicted*) in the conception phase,[[14]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_171016-18) the series was developed to subvert heist conventions and combine elements of the [action genre](Action_genre "Action genre"), [thrillers](Thrillers "Thrillers") and [surrealism](Surrealism "Surrealism"), while still being credible.[[11]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elperiodico_190718-14) Pina saw an advantage over typical heist films in that character development could span a considerably longer narrative arc.[[15]](Money_Heist#cite_note-partiv-19) Characters were to be shown from multiple sides to break the viewers' preconceptions of villainy and retain their interest throughout the show.[[15]](Money_Heist#cite_note-partiv-19) Key aspects of the planned storyline were written down at the beginning,[[16]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_190719-20) while the finer story beats were developed incrementally to not overwhelm the writers.[[17]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_190912-21) Writer Javier Gómez Santander compared the writing process to the Professor's way of thinking, "going around, writing down options, consulting engineers whom you cannot tell why you ask them that," but noted that fiction allowed the police to be written dumber when necessary.[[17]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_190912-21)

The beginning of filming was set for January 2017,[[13]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elconfidencial_170103-16) allowing for five months of pre-production.[[18]](Money_Heist#cite_note-dramaquarterly_180629a-22) The narrative was split into two parts for financial considerations.[[18]](Money_Heist#cite_note-dramaquarterly_180629a-22) The robbers' city-based code names, which Spanish newspaper *[ABC](ABC_(newspaper) "ABC (newspaper)")* compared to the colour-based code names in [Quentin Tarantino](Quentin_Tarantino "Quentin Tarantino")'s 1992 heist film *[Reservoir Dogs](Reservoir_Dogs "Reservoir Dogs")*,[[19]](Money_Heist#cite_note-abc_190716-23) were chosen at random in the first part,[[20]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elperiodico_190627-24) although places with high viewership resonance were also taken into account for the new robbers' code names in part 3.[[21]](Money_Heist#cite_note-xataka_190705-25) The first five lines of the pilot script took a month to write,[[18]](Money_Heist#cite_note-dramaquarterly_180629a-22) as the writers were unable to make the Professor or Moscow work as narrator.[[14]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_171016-18) Ultimately, Tokyo was chosen as an [unreliable narrator](Unreliable_narrator "Unreliable narrator"). Flashbacks and time-jumps increased the narrative complexity[[15]](Money_Heist#cite_note-partiv-19) and made the story more fluid for the audience.[[18]](Money_Heist#cite_note-dramaquarterly_180629a-22) The pilot episode required over 50 script versions until the producers were satisfied.[[22]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elpais_lcdp-26)[[23]](Money_Heist#cite_note-lanacion_190616-27) Later scripts would be finished once per week to keep up with filming.[[18]](Money_Heist#cite_note-dramaquarterly_180629a-22)

asting took place late in February 2016, spanning more than two months.[[24]](Money_Heist#cite_note-abc_170628-28) The characters were not fully fleshed out at the beginning of this process, and took shape based on the actors' performances.[[25]](Money_Heist#cite_note-tercer_grado-29) Casting directors Eva Leira and Yolanda Serrano were looking for actors with the ability to play empathetic robbers with believable love and family connections.[[26]](Money_Heist#cite_note-20minutos_190204-30) Antena 3 announced the ensemble cast in March 2017[[27]](Money_Heist#cite_note-antenacast-31) and released audition excerpts of most cast actors in the series' aftershow *Tercer Grado* and on their website.[[25]](Money_Heist#cite_note-tercer_grado-29)

The Professor was designed as a charismatic yet shy villain who could convince the robbers to follow him and make the audience sympathetic to the robbers' resistance against the powerful banks.[[28]](Money_Heist#cite_note-laprensa_190809-32) However, developing the Professor's role proved difficult, as the character did not follow archetypal conventions[[24]](Money_Heist#cite_note-abc_170628-28) and the producers were uncertain about his degree of brilliance.[[14]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_171016-18) While the producers found his Salva personality early on,[[14]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_171016-18) they were originally looking for a 50-year-old <Harvard> professor type with the looks of Spanish actor [José Coronado](Jos%C3%A9_Coronado "José Coronado").[[14]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_171016-18)[[29]](Money_Heist#cite_note-esquire_190125-33) The role was proposed to [Javier Gutiérrez](Javier_Guti%C3%A9rrez_%C3%81lvarez "Javier Gutiérrez Álvarez"), but he was already committed to starring in the film *[Campeones](Champions_(2018_film) "Champions (2018 film)")*.[[30]](Money_Heist#cite_note-34) Meanwhile, the casting directors advocated for [Álvaro Morte](%C3%81lvaro_Morte "Álvaro Morte"), whom they knew from their collaboration on the long-running Spanish soap opera *[El secreto de Puente Viejo](El_secreto_de_Puente_Viejo "El secreto de Puente Viejo")*, even though his prime-time television experience was limited at that point.[[29]](Money_Heist#cite_note-esquire_190125-33) Going through the full casting process and approaching the role through external analysis rather than personal experience, Morte described the professor as "a tremendous box of surprises" that "end up shaping this character because he never ceases to generate uncertainty," making it unclear for the audience if the character is good or bad.[[24]](Money_Heist#cite_note-abc_170628-28) The producers also found that his appearance of a primary school teacher gave the character more credibility.[[14]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_171016-18)

[Pedro Alonso](Pedro_Alonso "Pedro Alonso") was cast to play Berlin, whom *[La Voz de Galicia](La_Voz_de_Galicia "La Voz de Galicia")* would later characterize as a "cold, hypnotic, sophisticated and disturbing character, an inveterate macho with serious empathy problems, a white-collar thief who despises his colleagues and considers them inferior."[[31]](Money_Heist#cite_note-lavozdegalicia_170503-35) The actor's portrayal of the character was inspired by a chance encounter Alonso had the day before receiving his audition script, with "an intelligent person" who was "provocative or even manipulative" to him.[[32]](Money_Heist#cite_note-lefigaro_180621-36) Alonso saw high observation skills and an unusual understanding of his surroundings in Berlin, resulting in unconventional and unpredictable character behaviour.[[31]](Money_Heist#cite_note-lavozdegalicia_170503-35) Similarities between Berlin and [Najwa Nimri](Najwa_Nimri "Najwa Nimri")'s character Zulema in Pina's TV series *[Locked Up](Locked_Up_(TV_series) "Locked Up (TV series)")* were unintentional.[[33]](Money_Heist#cite_note-37) The family connection between the Professor and Berlin was not in the original script, but was built into the characters' backstory at the end of part 1 after Morte and Alonso had repeatedly proposed to do so.[[34]](Money_Heist#cite_note-38)

The producers found the protagonist and narrator, Tokyo, among the hardest characters to develop,[[18]](Money_Heist#cite_note-dramaquarterly_180629a-22) as they were originally looking for an older actress to play the character who had nothing to lose before meeting the Professor.[[25]](Money_Heist#cite_note-tercer_grado-29) [Úrsula Corberó](%C3%9Arsula_Corber%C3%B3 "Úrsula Corberó") eventually landed the role for bringing a playful energy to the table; her voice was heavily factored in during casting, as she was the first voice the audience hears in the show.[[25]](Money_Heist#cite_note-tercer_grado-29) [Jaime Lorente](Jaime_Lorente "Jaime Lorente") developed Denver's hallmark laughter during the casting process.[[25]](Money_Heist#cite_note-tercer_grado-29) Two cast actors had appeared in previous TV series by Álex Pina: [Paco Tous](Paco_Tous "Paco Tous") (Moscow) had starred in the 2005 TV series *[Los hombres de Paco](Los_hombres_de_Paco "Los hombres de Paco")*, and [Alba Flores](Alba_Flores "Alba Flores") (Nairobi) had starred in *Locked Up*. Flores was asked to play Nairobi without audition when Pina realised late in the conception phase that the show needed another female gang member.[[14]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_171016-18) For the role opposite to the robbers, [Itziar Ituño](Itziar_Itu%C3%B1o "Itziar Ituño") was cast to play Inspector Raquel Murillo, whom Ituño described as a "strong and powerful woman in a world of men, but also sensitive in her private life".[[35]](Money_Heist#cite_note-repubblica_180923-39) She took inspiration from *[The Silence of the Lambs](The_Silence_of_the_Lambs_(novel) "The Silence of the Lambs (novel)")* character [Clarice Starling](Clarice_Starling "Clarice Starling"), an FBI student with a messy family life who develops sympathies for a criminal.[[36]](Money_Heist#cite_note-40)

The actors learned of the show's renewal by Netflix before the producers contacted them to return.[[37]](Money_Heist#cite_note-41) In October 2018, Netflix announced the cast of part 3; the returning main cast included Pedro Alonso, raising speculation about his role in part 3.[[38]](Money_Heist#cite_note-42) Among the new cast members were Argentine actor [Rodrigo de la Serna](Rodrigo_de_la_Serna "Rodrigo de la Serna"), who saw a possible connection between his character's name and the Argentine football legend [Martín Palermo](Mart%C3%ADn_Palermo "Martín Palermo"),[[39]](Money_Heist#cite_note-43) and *Locked Up* star Najwa Nimri. Cameo scenes of Brazilian football star, and fan of the series, <Neymar>, as a monk were filmed for part 3, but were excluded from the stream without repercussions to the narrative until judicial charges against him had been dropped in late August 2019.[[40]](Money_Heist#cite_note-44)[[17]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_190912-21) A small appearance by Spanish actress [Belén Cuesta](Bel%C3%A9n_Cuesta "Belén Cuesta") in two episodes of part 3 raised fan and media speculation about her role in part 4.[[41]](Money_Heist#cite_note-45)

### Design

The show's look and atmosphere were developed by creator Álex Pina, director Jesús Colmenar, and director of photography Migue Amoedo, according to *[La Vanguardia](La_Vanguardia "La Vanguardia")* "the most prolific television trio in recent years".[[42]](Money_Heist#cite_note-lavanguardia_190719-46) Abdón Alcañiz served as art director.[[43]](Money_Heist#cite_note-alicanteplaza_180612-47) Their collaboration projects usually take a primary colour as a basis;[[43]](Money_Heist#cite_note-alicanteplaza_180612-47) *Money Heist* had red as "one of the distinguishing features of the series"[[44]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elpais_170503-48) that stood over the gray sets.[[45]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elpais_190711-49) Blue, green and yellow were marked as a forbidden colour in production design.[[45]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elpais_190711-49) To achieve "absolute film quality", red tones were tested with different types of fabrics, textures and lighting.[[46]](Money_Heist#cite_note-sensacine_190617-50) The iconography of the robbers' red jumpsuits mirrored the yellow prison dress code in *Locked Up*.[[44]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elpais_170503-48) For part 3, the Italian retail clothing company [Diesel](Diesel_(brand) "Diesel (brand)") modified the red jumpsuits to better fit the body and launched a clothing line inspired by the series.[[45]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elpais_190711-49) [Salvador Dalí](Salvador_Dal%C3%AD "Salvador Dalí") was chosen as the robbers' mask design because of Dalí's recognisable visage that also serves as an iconic cultural reference to Spain; [Don Quixote](Don_Quixote "Don Quixote") as an alternative mask design was discarded.[[47]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elpais_180712-51) This choice sparked criticism by the [Gala-Salvador Dalí Foundation](Gala-Salvador_Dal%C3%AD_Foundation "Gala-Salvador Dalí Foundation") for not requesting the necessary permissions.[[26]](Money_Heist#cite_note-20minutos_190204-30)

### Music

Main article: [Money Heist (soundtrack)](Money_Heist_(soundtrack) "Money Heist (soundtrack)")

The series' theme song, "[My Life Is Going On](My_Life_Is_Going_On "My Life Is Going On")," was composed by Manel Santisteban, who also served as composer on *Locked Up*. Santisteban approached Spanish singer, [Cecilia Krull](Cecilia_Krull "Cecilia Krull"), to write and perform the lyrics, which are about having confidence in one's abilities and the future.[[60]](Money_Heist#cite_note-oprahmag_190722-64) The theme song is played behind a title sequence featuring paper models of major settings from the series.[[60]](Money_Heist#cite_note-oprahmag_190722-64) Krull's main source of inspiration was the character Tokyo in the first episode of the series, when the Professor offers her a way out of a desperate moment.[[61]](Money_Heist#cite_note-lavoz_190917-65) The lyrics are in English as the language that came naturally to Krull at the time of writing.[[61]](Money_Heist#cite_note-lavoz_190917-65)

The Italian [anti-fascist](Anti-fascist "Anti-fascist") song "[Bella ciao](Bella_ciao "Bella ciao")" plays multiple times throughout the series and accompanies two emblematic key scenes: at the end of the first part the Professor and Berlin sing it in preparation for the heist, embracing themselves as resistance against the establishment,[[62]](Money_Heist#cite_note-faz_180802-66) and in the second part it plays during the thieves' escape from the Mint, as a metaphor for freedom.[[63]](Money_Heist#cite_note-bellaciao-67) Regarding the use of the song, Tokyo recounts in one of her narrations, "The life of the Professor revolved around a single idea: Resistance. His grandfather, who had [fought against the fascists in Italy](Italian_resistance_movement "Italian resistance movement"), taught him the song, and he taught us."[[63]](Money_Heist#cite_note-bellaciao-67) The song was brought to the show by writer Javier Gómez Santander. He had listened to "Bella ciao" at home to cheer him up, as he had grown frustrated for not finding a suitable song for the middle of part 1.[[17]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_190912-21) He was aware of the song's meaning and history and felt it represented positive values.[[17]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elmundo_190912-21) "Bella ciao" became a summer hit in Europe in 2018, mostly due to the popularity of the series and not the song's grave themes.[[62]](Money_Heist#cite_note-faz_180802-66)

### Season 2: Parts 3 and 4 (2019–2020)

Part 3 begins three years after the heist on the Royal Mint of Spain, showing the robbers enjoying their lives paired-up in diverse locations. However, when <Europol> captures Rio with an intercepted phone, the Professor picks up Berlin's old plans to assault the [Bank of Spain](Bank_of_Spain "Bank of Spain") to force Europol to hand over Rio to prevent his torture. He and Raquel (going by "Lisbon") get the gang, including Mónica (going by "Stockholm"), back together, and enlist three new members: Palermo, Bogotá and Marseille, with Palermo in charge. Flashbacks to the Professor and Berlin outline the planned new heist and their different approaches to love. The disguised robbers sneak into the heavily guarded bank, take hostages and eventually gain access to the gold and state secrets. At the same time, the Professor and Lisbon travel in an <RV> and then an ambulance while communicating with the robbers and the police. The robbers thwart a police breach of the bank, forcing the police, led by Colonel Luis Tamayo and pregnant inspector Alicia Sierra, to release Rio to the robbers. Nairobi is injured by a police [sniper](Sniper "Sniper")'s shot to the chest. With another police assault on the bank coming, and believing Lisbon has been executed by the police, the Professor radios Palermo and declares [DEFCON 2](DEFCON_2 "DEFCON 2"). The robbers respond by firing a rocket at the armored police vehicle that is advancing on the bank, turning the robbers from folk heroes to killers in the eyes of the public. Part 3 concludes by showing Lisbon alive and in custody, and Tokyo narrating that the Professor had fallen for a trap. She concludes that because of the Professor's miscalculation, "the war had begun."

Part 4 begins with the robbers rushing to save Nairobi's life. While Tokyo stages a coup d'état and takes over command from Palermo, the Professor and Marseille deduce that Lisbon must still be alive and being interrogated by Sierra in the police command post tent outside the bank. They persuade Tamayo's assistant, Antoñanzas, to help them so the Professor can establish a 48-hour truce with the police. As the group manages to save Nairobi's life, the restrained Palermo attempts to reassert command by colluding with Gandía, the restrained chief of security for the Bank of Spain. Gandía escapes, begins communications with the police from within a [panic room](Panic_room "Panic room") inside the bank, and participates in a violent cat-and-mouse game with the gang. Palermo reverses course, regains the trust of the group, and rejoins them. Gandía shoots Nairobi in the head, killing her instantly, but the gang later recapture him. As the police prepare another assault on the bank, the Professor exposes to the public the unlawful torture of Rio and Lisbon's detention and interrogation. Sierra is fired and begins pursuing the Professor on her own. The Professor enlists external help to free Lisbon after she is transferred from the command post tent to the Supreme Court building. Part 4 concludes with Lisbon rejoining the gang inside the bank, and with Sierra finding the Professor's hideout, then holding him at gunpoint.

### Season 3: Part 5 Volumes 1 and 2 (2021)

Part 5 Volume 1 begins with Sierra finding the Professor and knocking him out, then tying him up and interrogating him. Gandia wants to exact revenge on the gang, so Tamayo has him join the assault by the soldiers. After finding out the Professor has been caught but that Sierra has not notified the police, Lisbon tells the gang they will not give up. Benjamin and Marseille find the Professor, and Sierra knocks them out and ties them up. When Sierra struggles to deliver her baby, she frees the Professor, Marseille, and Benjamin so they can help. Sierra gives birth to a daughter, whom she names Victoria. Arturo Roman, a hostage in both the Royal Mint and the Bank of Spain, had an affair with Stockholm before the first heist, and Arturo's reminders anger Denver. When Arturo, the governor of the bank, and other hostages start a rebellion, Stockholm shoots Arturo, who is released so he can receive medical care. In a flashback, Berlin convinces his son Rafael to help him steal 12 kilograms of gold with Tatiana, Bogota, and Marseille. In the present, the gang starts fighting the soldiers, with Helsinki sustaining a severe injury. Stockholm feels guilt over shooting Arturo, who is her son's birth father, and takes morphine while nursing Helsinki, which leaves her unable to aid in the gang's defense against the attacking soldiers. Part 5 Volume 1 concludes with Tokyo sacrificing herself to defeat Gandia and the soldiers.

In Part 5 Volume 2, Sierra runs away and the Professor and Marseille chase after her. Initially enemies, the Professor and Sierra soon become allies as they face their common enemy – the police. When they go back to the stormwater tank, they see the gold has already been delivered to them by the gang. However, the police find the stormwater tank and arrests the Professor, Sierra, Benjamin and Marseille. They escape, but find the gold missing. It is revealed that the gold is stolen by Rafael and Tatiana because she broke up with Berlin in the past to be with Rafael. In the present, Tatiana and Rafael bury the gold. Palermo and the Professor discover that it is their doing, but at this time, the army captured the gang. The Professor gives Sierra a note for Rafael, and convinces her to find the gold as that is their only hope while he drives to the bank. When he enters the bank, Tamayo taunts him and interrogates each gang member separately. Denver goes first, but does not reveal anything and is escorted to the police tent. The gang reveals to the public the gold has already been removed from the bank, leading to public panic and an economic meltdown, putting Spain in danger of bankruptcy. Sierra is able to locate the stolen gold. Outside the bank, the gold has arrived in trucks, but the Professor says it is gold-coated [brass](Brass "Brass"). They are taken out of the bank in body bags, and it is revealed they are alive as the Professor convinced Tamayo to stop the chase; the return of the "gold" has stabilized the country's economy. 24 hours after the heist, the gang reunite at an air base. Everyone receives new passports as Rafael and Tatiana return the gold to the gang with a promise that they will receive a share. The gang leaves the air base, having successfully robbed the Bank of Spain.

Although the show's first two parts were popular, the domestic market in Spain failed to convince Antena 3 to continue the series and it was shelved until international response escalated to the point where the cast and crew were called back for another two seasons.[[126]](Money_Heist#cite_note-boss_hunting-131)

In numerous incidents, real heist men wore the show's red costumes and Dalì masks in their attacks or copied the fictional robbers' infiltration plans.[[3]](Money_Heist#cite_note-newstatesman_180824-4)[[22]](Money_Heist#cite_note-elpais_lcdp-26)[[127]](Money_Heist#cite_note-abc_190807-132) The robbers' costumes were banned at the 2019 [Limassol Carnival Festival](Limassol_Carnival_Festival "Limassol Carnival Festival") as a security measure as a result.[[128]](Money_Heist#cite_note-133) The series was used in an attack on YouTube, when hackers removed the most-played song in the platform's history, "<Despacito>", and left an image of the show instead.[[129]](Money_Heist#cite_note-134) In unrelated reports, a journalist from Turkish TV channel AkitTV and an [Ankaran](Ankara "Ankara") politician have both warned against the show for supposedly encouraging terrorism and being "a dangerous symbol of rebellion".[[3]](Money_Heist#cite_note-newstatesman_180824-4)
